body.text: Victorian election live: Voters head to polls as early voting centres open
Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will hold the balance of power in the state for the next four years.
Early voting opens today across Victoria, as the major parties continue their campaigns across the state.
Follow our live coverage below:

Bikie allegedly standing over labour hire company
At the Big Build royal commission, we're listening in on the second day of testimony from bikie Joel Leavitt.
We've taken a look at some of Leavitt's bank statements leading up to the $165,000 invoice he sent to BK Labour.
It appears he was financially struggling with his bank account figures dropping into the negatives at times or hovering around double digits.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis has put to Leavitt that he did not in fact do any work for BK Labour and that the invoice was a standover tactic to get a large sum of money at a time Leavitt "needed it badly".
"If that's the way you want to look at it commissioner, that's very much in your right to look at it that way," Leavitt says.
He hasn't been able to detail the exact work he did for this $165,000 invoice or the duration of the job.
At one stage he suggested it could have been just hours of work, which the commissioner pointed out would equate to him charging about $20,000 an hour for his services.
"Maybe I would have [charged that]. If a client's willing to pay, why not? Everyone likes money. I'm sure youse are on good money for this," he says.

The commission indicates it has evidence to suggest the money was a standover tactic and suggests it was for one of two reasons, either Leavitt had information on BK Labour that it would want kept quiet, which he denies.
Or that he stood over the labour hire company with some sort of explicit or implied violence.
Leavitt asked to seek legal advice before answering and a 10 minute break was called.
Seats in focus: Hawthorn

Hawthorn has been won by Labor just twice in its almost 140-year history. The first was in John Cain Sr's final election as leader in 1955 and the second in Daniel Andrews's landslide re-election in 2018. In the latter case, incumbent Liberal MP John Pesutto was live on the ABC's panel during coverage of that election as his defeat became clear.

Pesutto had succeeded former premier Ted Baillieu as local member at the 2014 election after serving as an adviser in his government. Pesutto eventually returned to parliament in 2022, recovering his seat with a slim margin, defeating both the Labor incumbent and an independent candidate who received support from Climate 200. He became leader of the Liberal Party after that election, defeating Brad Battin by just one vote.

In March 2023, Liberal MLC Moira Deeming addressed an anti-trans rally, which was also attended by neo-Nazis. Pesutto responded by moving to expel her from the party room. Deeming launched a defamation suit against her former leader and the conflict became a proxy for factional tensions in the party room, eventually leading to Pesutto's removal from the leadership in December 2024.

The seat has an increasingly large proportion of renters but also some of the highest rents in Melbourne. One of the Labor government's proposed "activity centres" will see more housing built around Hawthorn and Camberwell's public transport hubs.
This has attracted fierce opposition and may further reduce Labor's already slim chance of regaining the seat.
Future of regional Victorian food relief centres in jeopardy ahead of election
In the 2025 state government budget, Regional Food Security Alliance received $6 million over two years for its relief centres in Wodonga, Bendigo, Geelong, Shepparton, Mildura and Warrnambool.
But neither Labor nor the Coalition has committed to extending the grant.
It puts a service supplying 100,000 meals a week to Victorians in need in jeopardy.

As we've mentioned, the Victorian Electoral Commission says this is the biggest state election ever, with 4.7 million people eligible to vote.
About 60 per cent of those people are expected to vote before election day.
Labor's Big Red Bus rolls onto the pitch
Labor's campaign bus rolls on today, with Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams and Minister Anthony Carbines hitching a ride to Melbourne Rectangular Stadium.
The trip down to the stadium served as tool for Labor to illustrate the job cuts it says a Coalition government will bring.
"Even at a capacity of 30,000, that is still less than the number of people that Jess Wilson will need to sack in order to meet her promises," Williams said.
Citing research by the Australia Institute, Williams said Coalition cuts would see the sacking of 12,000 health workers, 5,000 nurses and 5,900 teachers.
Williams called any argument that the cuts would be to non-essential public sector jobs was "a fallacy".
When asked if Labor was planning to trim the public service workforce, Williams said the party would "continue to make sensible decisions".
"You've already seen in our [Victorian Public Service] numbers where we can, but not a reduction that will hit frontline services, there is a limit," she said.

TAFE body wants $2.5 billion investment
The Victorian TAFE Associaion (VTA) has released its wishlist ahead of the state election.
The VTA wants a $2.5 billion investment into TAFE infrastructure over the next 10 years.
It also wants funding for 10,000 addition TAFE places per year and aims to establish TAFE as a first choice provider for government departments and major projects.
VTA CEO Alex White wants the next government to make TAFE funding a priority.

"The aged care and social workers, many of the nurses and early childhood educators, and the tradies that this state will need over the course of the next decade will all be trained by a public TAFE," he says.
"Many mid-career workers also turn to TAFE to upskill or retrain, including increasingly due to AI-related job pressure.
"If we want more homes built, stronger healthcare services, and better public infrastructure including well-built roads, we must invest in training our workforce well."

''Crime on the streets, cost-of-living, a lot of things that just become personal for individuals,” Peter said. ''Whether the Liberals are able to do a lot about it … it's all about money, do they have any money for it.''

Seats in focus: Hastings
The areas covered by Hastings have leaned conservative over many years, but the seat has been closely contested during the long periods of Labor dominance of Victorian politics.

Going into the 2022 election, Hastings was one of the most marginal seats in the state after a redistribution cut the already slim Liberal margin to almost nothing. Longtime member Neale Burgess opted to retire and Labor ran actor and TV personality Paul Mercurio, who had been serving on the local council for the preceding two years. That recruitment paid off and Mercurio won the seat, one of two unexpected gains for Labor from seats held by the Liberals.

Going into the 2026 election the seat will once again likely be a closely fought contest between all three parties. Will Mercurio’s star power be enough to offset both an unpopular government and demographics favourable to One Nation?

As well as its high proportion of people with Australian or British ancestry, more than 91 per cent said they spoke English at home — the highest in the state. It also has some of the lowest rates of university education but the highest proportion of residents with a vocational qualification. Household incomes are slightly below the statewide average.
Commissioner's warning seems to have impact
There was a 10-minute break so bikie Joel Leavitt could seek some legal advice following Commissioner Chris Kourakis's warning.
When the hearing resumed, Leavitt answered the first question in detail and recalled events he was unable to recall yesterday.
"In the first answer you've given back, you have remembered some circumstances surrounding the invoice. What happened in the 10 minutes to revive your recollection?" commissioner Kourakis asked.
"I'm doing the best …. to recall how JBL consulting was ran," Leavitt says.
"As I said, my memory is not the best. I've been through more than most have in this room will ever go through in their whole life in three years so I am doing my best to recall on what I can."
Questions are being asked about a $165,000 invoice Leavitt issued to labour hire company BK Labour.
Why is Enver Erdogan now running in Eastern Victoria Region?

Can you please find out why the ALPs number 1 candidate for the Eastern Region (Gippsland) is Enver ERDOGAN, who, when I googled him, is the current Northern Metropolitan MLC and Minister for Finance Minister for Casino, Gaming and Liquor Regulation Minister for Government Services. The nomination says he lives in Greenvale, which is near Melbourne airport. Why is he moving laterally? Does he now live in Gippsland or is intending to move to Gippsland? What credentials does he have to represent Gippslanders? Or is this just another case of treating Gippslanders as mugs and no one will care. I care. Can he honestly say he is across what matters to Gippslanders?
- Dianne
Hi Dianne,
Thanks for your message.
The answer to this is that Labor see Eastern Victoria Region as more winnable.

As our state political reporter Rachel Eddie wrote last month, a handshake agreement moved Erdogan to the safer top position in Eastern Victoria, which covers Gippsland, with the existing MP there Tom McIntosh taking his place.
But the factional deal, designed to spare Erdogan, even angered some local Labor members.
Sonny Stephens, Labor's candidate in the lower house seat Gippsland East, in August launched a petition to keep McIntosh in the top position in Eastern Victoria.
At the time, Stephens told the ABC she had heard from members a "frustration with a process that doesn't appear to reward effort".
"The emotion that a decision like this generates among the members is just a terrible thing. It's not what you want in the run-up to the election," she said.
Warning to bikie about evading questions in royal commission
Commissioner Chris Kourakis has given bikie Joel Leavitt a stern warning that it is an offence to fail to answer questions put to him under examination at the Big Build royal commission.

"The only reason I'm saying this is to warn you that a finding could be made that you’ve made what some people would see as outlandish claims of … having no memory over periods of years in an attempt to avoid answering the questions," he says.
Leavitt had moments earlier told the commission he was seeing a psychologist to help with memory loss from around 2021 and 2022, which he attributed to PTSD.
He says that during the time a gang squad had a contract on his life, he was also shot.
"I am doing the best to my ability commissioner, to get this thing going, I don't know what else to say. It f***ed me up," he says.
Joel Leavitt returns to give evidence at Big Build royal commission
Victoria's Big Build royal commission is back in session with bikie Joel Leavitt back to give more evidence.
Yesterday, the inquiry was shown a series of text messages that exposed the efforts of a CFMEU organiser to ensure Leavitt was hired on a government building site.
Mr Leavitt had difficulties recalling events from 2021 and 2022 responding with "I don't recall" to most questions he was asked.

Policy in focus: Data centres
Data centres have become an increasingly hot topic politically, both in Australia and internationally.
Local councils and neighbourhoods have been increasingly wary about data centres being built near them, with calls for a moratorium on new approvals.
Nowhere has this been clearer than in West Footscray, where community pushback to power poles caused tech giant NextDC to delay expansions to its data centre.
The pushback from locals against data centres has found support from both the Greens and One Nation.

The Greens have called for an immediate moratorium on all new AI data centre projects and compensation for affected communities, while One Nation has pledged a ban on data centres on agricultural land and to protect neighbourhoods with stricter regulations and community consultation.
But Labor and the Coalition have been more muted in their response to data centres.

Labor have promised stricter regulations around locations, drinking water and energy usage. The Coalition has also promised to more tightly regulate data centres and create buffer zones around residential areas.
But neither party has pledged a ban or moratorium. With the state staring down the barrel of a major debt hole, the financial incentives behind data centres may become even more important.
The government said the data sector delivered $5.8 billion in capital expenditure into Victoria in 2025.

The Victorian Treasury also said in its budget papers that data centres will feature heavily in the state's economic future, with the value of commercial building approvals related to data centres exploding in Victoria.

In a property category the Victorian treasury says mainly comprises data centres, figures show approval value rising from just $1.2 billion in the year-to-September 2024, to $8.96 billion in the year-to-September 2026.

In a release in January, the Carroll government said AI could bring $30 billion in GSP (Gross State Product, the state equivalent of GDP) over the next 10 years, underpinned by projects such as NextDC's $2 billion AI factory in Fisherman's Bend.
Let us know what you think about data centres, and if the AI debate will be shaping your vote in the coming election.
Key Event
Greens want crackdown on AI surveillance
The Victorian Greens are pushing for a ban on AI surveillance in supermarkets and shops, calling the practice "creepy".
The proposed ban would cover facial recognition technology, biometric scanning and AI workplace monitoring.
Greens leader Ellen Sandell says governments have failed to keep up with advancements in technology.
"People should be able to do their shopping or go to work without the fear of their images and behaviour being used against them or given to tech giants," she says.
The Greens also want to ban AI-generated images from real estate advertising.
The party says the responsibility should be on real estate agents to advertise properties accurately.
Seats in focus: Greenvale

Greenvale was created ahead of the 2022 election mostly out of the now abolished seat of Yuroke as well as parts of the continuing seat of Broadmeadows. The areas covered by this seat historically strongly support the Labor Party and have often done so with double-digit two-party-preferred margins.

Yuroke’s MP Ros Spence, opted to contest the other new seat of Kalkallo to the north and secondary school teacher Iwan Walters was selected to contest Greenvale. As with other seats in Melbourne’s northern suburbs, Labor suffered a large swing, the largest of any major party contest in the state at almost 15 per cent. These swings were particularly pronounced in Roxburgh Park and Meadow Heights.
While the statewide headwinds are against the government, this area’s Labor history means it is far from certain the party will lose it.
Key Event
Jess Wilson hands out how-to-vote cards in Kew
There were plenty of voters in Kew in Melbourne's east making the most of early voting, and local candidates didn't miss the chance to campaign directly to some voters.
Liberal leader Jess Wilson was on hand, attracting plenty of media attention as she handed out how-to-vote cards to people as they walked past.
Standing to her right isindependent candidate Sophie Torney, who is seeking to make history as the first ever non-Liberal Member for Kew.
Torney ran against Wilson in the 2022 election, but came third, taking 21.1 per cent of votes to Jess Wilson's unassailable 44.3 per cent.

The logistics behind Victoria's biggest ever election
More than 4.7 million Victorians are set to vote by November 28, the largest number of voters on record.
But with millions of votes flowing in from about 1,700 election day voting centres, the logistics behind running the election are more complex than ever.

Key Event
Early voting centres open across Victoria
While election day isn't until November 28, Victorians were already lining up outside Melbourne Town Hall this morning as early voting opened.
These voters aren't alone either. The Victorian Electoral Commission says approximately 60 per cent of voters will cast their vote early.
Early voting centres will operate from 9am to 6pm each day until Friday, November 27, except for Sunday, November 22, when all voting centres are closed.

Welcome to the Victorian election blog
Good morning and welcome to our coverage of the Victorian election.
Early voting centres open their doors today, with more than half of eligible Victorians expected to cast their vote before election day.
The major parties are on the campaign trail today, while the public hearings for the Big Build royal commission roll on.
